speaker: SFX
text: OPENING JINGLE: hand percussion, upright bass, the sound of two cups placed on a table.

speaker: NORA
text: The café has given us the corner table with the table leg that doesn't quite reach the floor. If you hear a clunk, that is not a microphone problem. It's a furniture opinion.

speaker: JAIME
text: Welcome to La Cosa Exacta. Today is a call-in episode about something that makes kind people uncomfortable: sometimes the most helpful thing is to stop talking.

speaker: NORA
text: I would like everyone to acknowledge that Jaime has asked me to stop talking while we're broadcasting a talk show.

speaker: JAIME
text: For research. You're allowed to continue in a minute.

speaker: NORA
text: Our first guest is Mercedes, an adult interpreter trainee. Last week she came to a simulation where the patient actor asked whether a form would guarantee a successful outcome. The interpreter knew several plausible answers from other jobs. Mercedes, what happened?

speaker: MERCEDES
text: The interpreter actor said, in Spanish, “Sí, si firma, todo estará bien.” But the clinician had said only, “This form allows us to discuss the procedure; it doesn't guarantee the outcome.”

speaker: NORA
text: That is an expensive extra promise.

speaker: MERCEDES
text: It sounded comforting. Everyone was anxious. That's exactly why it was tempting.

speaker: JAIME
text: If the interpreter is nervous too, what's the useful move?

speaker: MERCEDES
text: Preserve the speaker's actual degree of certainty, and ask for clarification transparently when a phrase isn't understood. Do not invent reassurance. I'm learning how to say that without turning every minute into a debate.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do a small recorded comparison with actors. One line is faithful and one changes a condition. No private clinical records are involved.

speaker: ACTOR, CLINICIAN
text: We can explain the options, but I can't promise which option will work for you.

speaker: ACTOR, INTERPRETER
text: Podemos explicar las opciones, pero no puedo prometer cuál funcionará para usted.

speaker: ACTOR, INTERPRETER
text: Si escoge esta opción, seguro que le funcionará.

speaker: SFX
text: An intentionally long pause. A spoon rolls across the table.

speaker: NORA
text: Which one should make our listeners uncomfortable?

speaker: JAIME
text: Not the silence. That spoon is far more troubling than the silence.

speaker: MERCEDES
text: The second interpretation. It erased the limits on what the clinician knew and gave personalized advice that was never spoken.

speaker: NORA
text: Exactly. The performance of certainty is not certainty. Still, can we make this entertaining without laughing at the patient?

speaker: MERCEDES
text: We can laugh at ourselves. Everyone thinks they can tell what a person means by the way they look. My aunt can turn one raised eyebrow into a weather forecast. At work, eyebrows are not an authorized translation channel.

speaker: JAIME
text: That's going on a mug.

speaker: SFX
text: SHORT MUSIC BRIDGE. A caller enters.

speaker: CALLER ELENA
text: I have a different problem. In a practice legal conversation, I heard, “The court has scheduled a hearing.” The trainee interpreted, “The judge has decided.” I caught it because my stomach dropped. But after the session I was afraid to say anything. The person who said it looked so confident.

speaker: NORA
text: Confidence has excellent tailoring. Facts don't always wear jackets.

speaker: MERCEDES
text: We can name the exact difference without humiliating anyone. Scheduled means there will be a proceeding. Decided means the outcome has been determined. Those are not the same. And we should be careful with the specific procedure and jurisdiction instead of guessing the consequences.

speaker: JAIME
text: The interesting thing is that nobody needed a difficult vocabulary word to make that error. A verb did it.

speaker: NORA
text: We have a recurring question from listeners: why not correct everything immediately, even a small change in tone?

speaker: MERCEDES
text: Because a professional response depends on the setting and applicable protocol. The aim is accurate communication and transparent repair, not becoming another participant who controls the conversation. When you're learning, the question is what the speaker actually authorized you to say.

speaker: NORA
text: Let me make a confession. Before this show, I translated my grandmother's message to the family chat. She said, “I'll probably be there after lunch.” I sent, “She is coming at one.”

speaker: JAIME
text: Did she arrive at one?

speaker: NORA
text: She arrived at four with an enormous cake and said she'd been very clear. She was correct. “Probably” wasn't decorative. “After lunch” wasn't a clock.

speaker: MERCEDES
text: Did she forgive you?

speaker: NORA
text: She gave me the cake. Then she made me carry it up three flights of stairs. That was her formal review process.

speaker: SFX
text: A PHONE DINGS.

speaker: JAIME
text: We have an email from a listener asking whether they can just put uncertain words in quotation marks.

speaker: MERCEDES
text: Quotation marks don't repair a changed assertion. The listener needs to preserve the actual uncertainty. A careful rendering may sound less elegant than a confident invention. That's fine. It's doing the job.

speaker: NORA
text: Before we go, I want to try something. I'll read a sentence; we won't provide the answer immediately. Our listeners can think for five seconds and decide what must stay in the interpretation.

speaker: NORA
text: I may have seen the person near the station, but I'm not sure it was the same person.

speaker: SFX
text: Five seconds of real silence in the production mix. Only the air conditioning is audible.

speaker: JAIME
text: Things worth keeping: the possibility, the location, and the uncertainty about identity. Nothing about ownership. Nothing about guilt.

speaker: NORA
text: That was an unusually good summary from a man who insists our espresso machine is sentient.

speaker: JAIME
text: It refused to give me coffee this morning. That's evidence.

speaker: MERCEDES
text: That's a machine malfunction. You should get it repaired before you call a witness.

text: THEME RETURNS. THE TABLE LEG CLUNKS A FINAL TIME.

text: This has been La Cosa Exacta. Keep the words that belong to the speaker—even the small ones that aren't trying to impress anyone.
